You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failing test case calls `HelpFormatter.printHelp()` with an option having a very long description and a set width of 20 characters. According to the bug report, this caused an infinite loop in the wrapping code, ultimately resulting in an OutOfMemoryError.

The code flow starts at `printHelp(String, Options)`, which delegates to `printHelp(int, String, String, Options, String, boolean)`, then calls `printHelp(PrintWriter, int, String, String, Options, int, int, String, boolean)`. This method handles printing the usage, header, options, and footer. The options printing occurs in `printOptions()`, which calls `renderOptions()`.

Within `renderOptions()`, option strings with their descriptions are constructed and then passed to `renderWrappedText()` for line wrapping according to the specified width. 

`renderWrappedText()` tries to find a wrap position in the text and append line breaks accordingly. It uses a loop to keep wrapping the text until all is processed or no wrap is needed. However, if the `findWrapPos()` method repeatedly returns the same wrap position (`pos == lastPos`), this causes an infinite loop.

To avoid this, `renderWrappedText()` has a check: if the wrap position does not move forward in the string between iterations, it throws a RuntimeException with the message indicating the text is too long for a line to prevent the infinite loop (CLI-162).

The report states that the original version did not have this exception and instead entered an infinite loop. The current implementation seen here contains this exception throw, indicating that this was added later to address this exact issue.

Thus, originally the loop would never break when a single word exceeded the width, causing an infinite loop. The bug occurs because the wrapping algorithm cannot break a single word that is longer than the allowed width, so the wrap position does not advance and the while loop never finishes.

This explains the infinite loop seen in the test when wrapping a very long word or description with a small column width.

Relevant methods:
- `printHelp(...)` delegating methods
- `printOptions()`
- `renderOptions()` that constructs the string with option descriptions
- `renderWrappedText()` that attempts word wrapping and is the site of the infinite loop when wrap position does not advance  

The recent bug reports are unrelated to text wrapping or line breaking and do not provide additional clues.

Summary: The infinite loop is caused by the wrapping code's inability to break long words that exceed the width, causing the wrap position to not advance and the loop to run infinitely. The current code includes a safeguard that throws a RuntimeException to prevent this in known problematic cases. The root cause is that the wrapping strategy does not handle very long single words gracefully.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
